issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court cannot recall an earlier order by reconsidering its merits when the record discloses no self-evident error.
material_facts: The High Court had dismissed revision petitions challenging the trial court’s decision to implead a neighbour in a suit concerning a municipal notice and construction.

On review, the High Court considered documents that had not been before the trial court and reconsidered whether the neighbour was a proper party, then recalled its earlier order and directed fresh consideration.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had reconsidered the merits and that no mistake apparent on the face of the record justified review.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its limited review jurisdiction. The Supreme Court set aside the order recalling the earlier order and allowed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Review jurisdiction is extremely limited: an order may be reviewed for a mistake apparent on the face of the record, meaning a self-evident mistake that requires no search to identify. Review is not an appeal in disguise and does not permit rehearing on the merits. Although the dispute concerned impleadment under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Supreme Court did not independently decide the merits of that question. No earlier case was relied on by the Supreme Court in stating the review principle.

predicates.appeal_from_review_order: An affected party appealed from an order made while reviewing an earlier judicial order.
predicates.merits_reconsidered: The reviewing court reconsidered the merits of its earlier order rather than limiting itself to correcting an apparent record error.
predicates.no_self_evident_error: The earlier order contained no self-evident mistake apparent from the record that required no search to identify.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a review order, the reviewing court reconsidered the merits, and no self-evident error existed, the review order must be set aside.
